lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003eAl avanzar por el per:
"

Moving across the period, electronegativity increases and the conjugate base is stabilized: CH₃⁻ (50) < NH₂⁻ (38) < HO⁻ (15.7). Moving down the group, size and polarizability dominate: S⁻ spreads the charge over a larger volume, so ethanethiol (10.6) is more acidic than ethanol (15.9).

"
lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003eEn el \u003cb\u003eal:
"

In the alkoxide the charge stays on one O. In the phenoxide it is spread over the ring, and in the carboxylate between two equivalent O atoms: pKa 15.9 → 10.0 → 4.76. Each red cloud shows how many atoms share the charge: the more sites, the lower the charge density on each and the greater the stability.

"
lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003eLos pKa de los compue:
"

The pKa values of organic compounds span about 50 units: alkanes ≈ 50 · ammonia 38 · alkynes 25 · ketones (α-H) ≈ 19 · alcohols 16–17 · phenols 10 · carboxylic acids 3–5. The difference between ethane and acetic acid is ~1045 in Ka.

The bar on the right in “Graphs” ranks all the compounds; the dotted line marks the pKa of the conjugate acid of the chosen base: an acid below the line is almost completely deprotonated.

"
lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003ePara saber si una bas:
"

To know whether a base deprotonates an acid, compare the pKa values: if pKa(HB) > pKa(HA), the equilibrium favors the products (K > 1). Examples: phenol + HCO₃⁻ (6.35 < 10.0): hardly deprotonated; phenol + HO⁻: complete; ethanol + HO⁻: ≈ equilibrium (K ≈ 0.6); propanone + NH₂⁻: complete. With NaOH you get phenoxide, but not acetylide.

"

lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003eUn orbital con más \u:
"

An orbital with more s character is closer to the nucleus and holds the electron pair better: sp (50 % s) > sp² (33 %) > sp³ (25 %). Thus: ethane 50 → ethene 44 → ethyne 25. That is why the H of a terminal alkyne is removed with NaNH₂, but not with NaOH.

"
